lesson.subject: data-ai
lesson.title: Data Detectives
lesson.summary: Surveys and averages, honest charts, databases, Venn diagrams, chance experiments and trends over time.
learning_objectives: Run a survey and find the mean, mode and median
Spot an honest chart and read a database
Sort with a Venn diagram and describe a trend

standards.text: Interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs
Organise and present collected data visually to highlight relationships
Use data to highlight or propose cause-and-effect relationships and predict outcomes

success_criteria: I can find the mean, mode and median
I can tell whether a chart is honest
I can sort with a Venn diagram and describe a trend
lesson.real_life: Weather tables, cricket scores, class votes and library records all use data.

warm_up.prompt: What do we call a mistake in a program?

blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how can we trust what data tells us?
blocks.say: Today we collect, check and describe data. How can we trust what data tells us?

blocks.alt: A glass thermometer scale held up close, showing degrees Celsius
blocks.caption: A thermometer measures temperature. A data logger takes many readings.
blocks.credit: Photo by Matteo Fusco on Unsplash
blocks.say: A thermometer gives one reading. A data logger can take hundreds, all through the day.

blocks.text: Stop 1: Asking questions with a survey

blocks.markdown:
A **survey** asks the same question to many people.

The group we ask is the **sample**. A bigger, fairer sample is more reliable.
blocks.say: A data detective starts with a question. To find the answer we run a survey. We ask a group of people the same question and record each answer. The group we ask is called the sample. A bigger, fairer sample gives a more reliable answer. Here a class of twenty chose a favourite sport.

blocks.title: Favourite sport in class 4
blocks.caption: Twenty children voted. Cricket got the most.

question.prompt: In the sport survey, how many children chose football?

blocks.markdown:
The **mean** is the fair share: add up, then divide by how many.

The **mode** is the most common value. The **median** is the middle one.
blocks.say: Sometimes we want one number to describe a whole set of numbers. The mean is the fair share. Add the numbers up, then divide by how many there are. Three friends read 3, 5 and 7 books. Together that is 15. Shared fairly between three, each gets 5. So the mean is 5. The mode is the number that appears most often. The median is the middle number when they are in order.

scenes.caption: 3 + 5 + 7 = 15 books.
scenes.say: Three friends read 3, 5 and 7 books. That is 15 books altogether.

scenes.caption: Share 15 equally between 3.
scenes.say: Share them out equally between the three friends.

scenes.caption: 15 divided by 3 is 5. The mean is 5!
scenes.say: Each friend gets 5. So the mean number of books is 5.

question.prompt: Four friends score 2, 4, 6 and 8 in a game. What is the mean score?
question.hint: Add them up, then divide by 4.

blocks.title: Fatima's weather study
blocks.transcript: Fatima asks: how does the temperature change during the day? A data logger takes a reading every ten minutes. That is six readings an hour. The readings go into a table. Each row is one reading. She draws a line graph. It rises to a peak at three o'clock. She finds the mean, the mode and the median of the readings. A friend's chart starts at fifty. Small differences look huge. Fatima redraws it from zero. Now it tells the truth. She predicts tomorrow's peak. A prediction is a careful guess, not a fact.
blocks.caption: Fatima logs the weather and checks whether her chart is honest.

points: A survey asks the same question to a sample
Mean: add up, divide by how many
Mode is most common, median is the middle
blocks.say: Let us remember. A survey asks many people. The mean is the fair share, the mode is the most common and the median is the middle.

blocks.text: Stop 1: Charts that tell the truth

blocks.markdown:
An honest **bar chart** starts at **zero** and labels every bar.

Read the numbers, not just the height!
blocks.say: A chart should help people understand, not trick them. An honest bar chart starts its bars at zero, has a clear title, and labels each bar. A tricky chart might squash or stretch the scale so small differences look huge. Always read the numbers, not just the height of the bars. This chart shows rainy days in each month.

blocks.title: Rainy days per month
blocks.caption: July had the most rainy days.
blocks.say: Look at the bars. Which month is tallest?

question.prompt: In the rainy days chart, which month had the most rainy days?

blocks.title: Spot the trick
instructions: Draw a bar chart of 3 votes and 5 votes, starting at zero.
Now draw it starting at 2. How do the bars look different?
blocks.say: Try drawing the same votes two ways and compare them.

blocks.markdown: A **database** is an organised table. Each **row** is one item and each **column** is a **field**.
blocks.say: A database stores lots of information in an organised table. Each row is one thing, such as one book. Each column is one kind of fact, called a field, such as the title or the year. Computers can search and sort a database very quickly. Look at this small library database.

blocks.title: Library database: books read
blocks.caption: Book title and the number of times borrowed.

blocks.alt: A database can be searched and sorted in an instant.
blocks.caption: A database can be searched and sorted in an instant.
blocks.say: Computers can sort this table from the most borrowed to the least borrowed in an instant.

question.prompt: Which book was borrowed the most?

points: A database has rows and columns
blocks.say: Let us remember. Honest charts start at zero and are clearly labelled. A database stores facts in rows and columns.

The starting point of a scale.
An organised table of information.

blocks.markdown: A **Venn diagram** uses overlapping circles. The middle holds things with **both** properties.
blocks.say: A Venn diagram sorts things with two circles. Each circle holds things with one property. The overlap in the middle holds things that have both. Let us sort animals into those with wings and those that swim. A duck has wings and swims, so it goes in the overlap. An eagle has wings only. A fish swims only.

scenes.caption: Three animals to sort.
scenes.say: Here are the animals before sorting: duck, eagle, fish.

scenes.caption: Two circles: wings and swim.
scenes.say: The Venn diagram has a circle for wings and a circle for swimming.

scenes.caption: The duck goes in the middle.
scenes.say: The eagle goes in wings only. The fish goes in swim only. The duck goes in the overlap, because it has both.

question.prompt: Where does a duck go in the wings and swim Venn diagram?
question.explanation: A duck has wings and swims, so it goes in the middle.

blocks.markdown: A **chance experiment** repeats a test many times and records the results.
blocks.say: In a chance experiment we try something many times and record the results. If you toss a coin twenty times, you might get about ten heads. But not exactly ten! The more times you try, the closer the results usually get to what you expect. Data from experiments helps us decide how likely things are. Play a memory game to warm up, then try the experiment at home.

instructions: Make a tally of heads and tails.
Is it exactly 10 each? Is it close?
blocks.say: Toss a coin twenty times and keep a tally of heads and tails.

question.prompt: If we toss a coin 20 times we must get exactly 10 heads.
question.explanation: We expect about 10 but it can vary.

Repeat a chance experiment to see what happens

blocks.caption: Weather data helps us predict storms and rain.
blocks.credit: Photo by Dave Hoefler on Unsplash
blocks.say: Weather changes through the day. Storm clouds like these are a clue to rain, and data helps us predict it.

blocks.markdown: We can look for a **trend**: does the data go up, down or stay the same?
blocks.say: Some data changes over time, like the temperature through a week. We can record it in a table and look for a pattern. Does it go up, go down, or stay the same? Here is the midday temperature in Lahore across four days in autumn.

blocks.title: Midday temperature (degrees C)
blocks.caption: Temperatures rise each day.
blocks.say: Look at the table. The numbers get bigger each day.

question.prompt: What is the trend in the temperature?

blocks.markdown: Describe the story with numbers, then make a careful **prediction**.
blocks.say: A good detective tells the story of the data in a sentence. For example: the temperature rose by five degrees from Monday to Thursday. Then they ask a new question, like what might happen on Friday. A prediction must say it is a prediction, because we cannot be sure.

blocks.alt: The temperature rose from 28 to 33 degrees.
blocks.caption: The temperature rose from 28 to 33 degrees.
blocks.say: The temperature rose by five degrees from Monday to Thursday.

blocks.title: My weather table
materials: A thermometer or a weather app
instructions: Record the temperature at the same time for four days.
Write one sentence about the trend.
Make a careful prediction for tomorrow.
blocks.say: Now collect real data at home.

blocks.prompt: Can we be sure the temperature will be 34 on Friday?
blocks.answer_markdown: No. A prediction is a sensible guess from the pattern, but the weather can change.
